section_summary: This section (pages 1–72) of decimal file 894.4061 covers State Department correspondence, consular despatches, and industry communications regarding motion pictures in Japan between 1933 and 1938 (along with an out-of-sequence 1941 cable regarding blocked film earnings). It primarily documents the emergence of anti-American and anti-Soviet military and naval propaganda films in Japan emphasizing the impending 'crisis of 1935–1936', as well as the premiere and reception of the high-profile German-Japanese co-production 'The New Earth'. Additionally, it details American film industry reactions to Japanese state control, including Home Office censorship demands on Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer's 'The Good Earth', import prohibitions under the 1937 emergency trade legislation, and negotiations over proposed credit and bank-note financing schemes.

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum evaluating potential Japanese reactions to the exhibition of the film 'Madame Butterfly'.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Eugene H. Dooman)
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs evaluates a letter from W. J. Jarvin suggesting that sending the film 'Madame Butterfly' to the Orient would be unwise. The memorandum notes that the opera has been performed repeatedly in Japan without offense. It explains that Japanese audiences generally view romantic liaisons between Japanese women and Western men with disdain rather than sympathy, and concludes that exhibiting the film is unlikely to provoke any untoward incidents.
subfiles.title: FE Memorandum regarding Proposed Exhibition of "Madame Butterfly" in Japan

subfiles.about: Letter from W. J. Jarvin expressing concern over the exhibition of the film 'Madame Butterfly' in the Orient.
subfiles.from: W. J. Jarvin (Los Angeles, California)
subfiles.summary: W. J. Jarvin writes to the Department of State to express concern over permitting the film 'Madame Butterfly' to be shown in the Orient. He suggests that sending such a production abroad would be very unwise. The communication is referred to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs for assessment.
subfiles.title: Letter from W. J. Jarvin regarding "Madame Butterfly"

subfiles.about: Official reply stating that the U.S. government lacks legal authority to control the export of motion pictures.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs (for the Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: The Department of State acknowledges receipt of W. J. Jarvin's letter and enclosure concerning the film 'Madame Butterfly'. Hornbeck informs Jarvin that American law does not vest the federal government with control over the export of motion picture films. He notes, however, that the motion picture industry exercises a measure of supervisory control over its member organizations.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to W. J. Jarvin

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting an Embassy memorandum reviewing the Japanese patriotic propaganda film 'Daigorei' (The Great Order).
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits a memorandum by Embassy officer W. T. Turner reviewing the patriotic propaganda film 'Daigorei' (The Great Order), produced with Army and Navy cooperation under the auspices of the Osaka Mainichi and Tokyo Nichinichi. Turner describes the film's focus on the 'crisis of 1935–1936', world trade rivalry, the naval conference, and a heavily emphasized Soviet military menace against Manchuria and Mongolia. Speeches by Generals Senjuro Hayashi and Sadao Araki and diplomat Yosuke Matsuoka are highlighted, alongside themes of a united Asia led by Japan. Turner considers the production crude and puerile, noting thin theatre attendance and Soviet diplomatic protests in Pravda.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 886: Japanese Propaganda Moving Picture "Daigorei"

subfiles.about: Cross-reference file note referencing a report on a Japanese propaganda film shown in Santiago, Chile.
subfiles.from: Frank P. Atwood, Santiago
subfiles.summary: A document file note cross-referencing Report No. 110 from Santiago, Chile, dated August 20, 1934, by reporting officer Atwood. The underlying despatch concerns a Japanese propaganda film exhibited in Santiago. The original document is recorded under decimal file 893.01-Manchuria/1157.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Japanese Propaganda Film Exhibited in Santiago, Chile

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Kobe Despatch No. 410 regarding 'Japan Advancing Northward'.
subfiles.from: W. T. Turner, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: W. T. Turner summarizes Kobe's Despatch No. 410 regarding the patriotic film 'Japan Advancing Northward'. The memorandum highlights that the production depicts the United States as a potential military menace threatening Japan by air from Alaska and the Aleutian Islands.
subfiles.title: FE Memorandum on Kobe Despatch No. 410: "Japan Advancing Northward"

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on the naval-industrial propaganda film 'Hokushin-no-Nippon' (Japan Advancing Northward) and its anti-American and anti-Soviet themes.
subfiles.from: Howard Donovan, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.summary: Consul Howard Donovan reports on the 10-reel sound film 'Japan Advancing Northward' (Hokushin-no-Nippon), produced by Yokohama Cinema Company with Navy Department assistance and distributed by Saneisha. Viewed by Donovan and Vice Consul Carey J. Scott at the Shochikuza Theatre, the film covers northern resource development in Sakhalin and the Kuriles, Soviet fishery disputes in Kamchatka, and historical flights across the North Pacific. The final portion warns of potential American air raids against Japan via Alaska and Dutch Harbor during the 1935–1936 crisis, depicting the United States and Russia as two fists closing in on Japan. Enclosed are promotional clippings and program synopses from the Osaka Mainichi and the Shochikuza Theatre.
subfiles.title: Kobe Despatch No. 410: Motion Picture Film Entitled Hokushin-no-Nippon (Japan Advancing Northward)

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on the military propaganda and air defense film 'Air Attacks and Air Raid Protection' shown in Kobe.
subfiles.from: Howard Donovan, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.summary: Consul Howard Donovan reports on the exhibition of 'Air Attacks and Air Raid Protection' at the Kinema Club in Kobe, produced by the Asia Film Company. The film utilizes animated cartoons, bomb-drop simulations, and footage from Kobe civil defense maneuvers to illustrate aerial bombing and gas casualties. Strategic diagrams show bomber ranges from Soviet territory, Dutch Harbor, Manila, and Guam, identifying Russia and the United States as Japan's primary aerial adversaries. Donovan cites an editorial from the Japan Chronicle condemning the film for drumming up war hysteria, and notes that another ambitious film, 'Japan Stands Alone', is currently in preparation.
subfiles.title: Kobe Despatch No. 431: Showing of Military Propaganda Film at Kobe, Japan

subfiles.about: Telegram approving Tokyo Embassy's stance against American motion picture companies investing blocked earnings in Japanese national bonds.
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.summary: The Department of State replies to Tokyo Embassy telegrams Nos. 1369 and 1370 regarding American film distributor funds held in Japan. Colonel Frederick L. Herron of the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America reported that company managers decided to handle their assets individually, as some lacked accounts in the National City Bank. The Department approves the Embassy's advice against investing film revenues in Japanese national bonds and suggests re-emphasizing this policy as opportunity arises.
subfiles.title: State Department Telegram to Tokyo Embassy on American Film Company Funds

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on the naval sponsorship, budget, and themes of the forthcoming propaganda film 'Japan Stands Alone'.
subfiles.from: Howard Donovan, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.summary: Consul Howard Donovan provides advance intelligence on the production of 'Japan Stands Alone', promoted by Chuko Ikozaki. The film has a budget of 30,000 yen, funded primarily by the Japanese Navy's educational fund with a contribution from the Nihon Aikoku Domei. Being produced by the Teikoku Film Production Company at the Uzumasa studios in Kyoto, the picture portrays Japan as the solitary shield against Occidental aggression in Asia, casting the United States and its navy as Japan's chief adversaries.
subfiles.title: Kobe Despatch No. 443: Propaganda Film Sponsored by Japanese Navy

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Kobe Despatch No. 455 on 'Storm over the Far East'.
subfiles.from: W. T. Turner, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: W. T. Turner summarizes Kobe Despatch No. 455 concerning the patriotic sound film 'Storm over the Far East'. The memorandum notes that the production seeks to arouse public fervor over the 1935–1936 national emergency by depicting the American Navy and Russian Army as hostile forces. Turner emphasizes that the film was made with Imperial Guard detachment support and ex-servicemen's patronage, illustrating Japan's systematic utilization of motion pictures for national propaganda.
subfiles.title: FE Memorandum on Kobe Despatch No. 455: "Storm over the Far East"

subfiles.about: Despatch providing an exhaustive review of the naval propaganda film 'Storm in the Far East' shown at Kobe.
subfiles.from: Howard Donovan, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.summary: Consul Howard Donovan reports in detail on 'Storm in the Far East' (Kyokuto no Arashi), produced by Shinshin Kinema and shown at Kobe's Kinema Club to commemorate the 30th anniversary of the Russo-Japanese War. The film opens with an address by Vice Admiral Viscount Chosei Ogasawara and a fantasy sequence of the God of War attacking Tokyo, followed by a household discussion led by Dr. Hiroi explaining the 1935–1936 crisis, the abrogation of the Washington Naval Treaty, the Soviet air threat, and American Pacific fleet maneuvers. A major segment promotes Sino-Japanese unity through the story of Ko-Bunseki, a Chinese activist who abandons anti-Japanese agitation after observing a Japanese sailor selflessly rescue a drowning Chinese farmer. Donovan and Vice Consul Carey J. Scott noted genuine audience enthusiasm; promotional advertisements from the Osaka Mainichi are attached.
subfiles.title: Kobe Despatch No. 455: Showing of Naval Propaganda Film at Kobe, Japan

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Kobe Despatch No. 464 on '10,000 Ri of Battle Front in the Far East'.
subfiles.from: W. T. Turner, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
keywords: "10,000 Ri of Battle Front in the Far East"
subfiles.summary: W. T. Turner summarizes Kobe Despatch No. 464 regarding the propaganda film '10,000 Ri of Battle Front in the Far East'. The memorandum notes that while the production resembles previous patriotic compilations, it places even heavier emphasis on the perceived American menace.
subfiles.title: FE Memorandum on Kobe Despatch No. 464: "10,000 Ri of Battle Front in the Far East"

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on the military propaganda film '10,000 Leagues of the Battle Fronts in the Far East' screened in Osaka.
subfiles.from: Howard Donovan, American Consul, Kobe
keywords: "10,000 Leagues of the Battle Fronts in the Far East"
subfiles.summary: Consul Howard Donovan reports on '10,000 Leagues of the Battle Fronts in the Far East' (Kyokuto Sensen Ichiman-ri), shown at the Nippon Club in Osaka and attributed to the Shochiku News Department (though disclaimed by Shochiku Kinema). Composed of synchronized newsreel cuts and strategic maps, the film shows Japan's vital interests encircled by the United States, Soviet Russia, and the British naval base at Singapore. The narrator urges preparation for the 1936 emergency and underscores closer Sino-Japanese cooperation while highlighting American aircraft carriers and naval strength as the paramount danger. Donovan notes a crowded house but little audience enthusiasm, and encloses an advertisement from the Osaka Mainichi.
subfiles.title: Kobe Despatch No. 464: Showing of Military Propaganda Film at Osaka, Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference file note regarding the refusal of Japanese authorities to permit MGM representative Edward F. O'Connor to land in Yokohama.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: A document file note cross-referencing Tokyo Despatch No. 1662, dated February 6, 1936, by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew. The despatch reports that Edward F. O'Connor, dispatched from Singapore by Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer to serve as its Tokyo representative, was denied permission to land at Yokohama due to his conduct during a previous stay in Japan. The underlying paper is filed under 394.1124 O'Connor, Edward F./1.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Edward F. O'Connor Refused Landing Permission

subfiles.about: Cross-reference file note reporting on the status of the case involving Edward F. O'Connor's exclusion from Japan.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: A document file note cross-referencing Tokyo Despatch No. 1685, dated February 19, 1936, by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew. The despatch details the ongoing status of the case of Edward F. O'Connor, who was refused entry into Japan as the representative of Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer. The original record is filed under decimal file 394.1124 O'Connor, Edward F.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Status of Edward F. O'Connor Case

subfiles.about: Cross-reference file note concerning a request for statistical data on the Japanese motion picture industry for 1936.
subfiles.from: Carl H. Boehringer, Assistant Trade Commissioner, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: A document file note cross-referencing E. & T. Note No. 371 from Assistant Trade Commissioner Carl H. Boehringer in Tokyo, dated January 26, 1937. It references an inquiry of January 22 regarding 1936 Japanese feature film production figures and theatre sound installations. The note indicates that 1936 production figures are not yet compiled but should be obtainable by the end of February 1937. The underlying document is filed under 102.81 Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Statistics of Japanese Motion Picture Industry
subfiles.to: Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce / Department of State

subfiles.about: Cross-reference file note reporting on Japanese motion picture industry statistics communicated via Shanghai.
subfiles.from: Carl H. Boehringer, Assistant Trade Commissioner, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: A document file note cross-referencing E. & T. Note No. 371 from Assistant Trade Commissioner Carl H. Boehringer in Tokyo, dated January 25, 1937. It records that domestic feature film production data for 1936 were not yet available at the time of mailing to Shanghai for Bureau transmission, though trade contacts expected figures by late February. The original report is filed under 102.81 Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Statistics of Japanese Motion Picture Industry (Transmittal)
subfiles.to: Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce / Department of State

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on the premiere and critical reception of the German-Japanese co-production film 'The New Earth' directed by Arnold Fanck.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports on the premiere of 'The New Earth' (Atarashiki Tsuchi / Die Tochter des Samurai), sponsored by the Kokusai Bunka Shinkokai and Towa Shoji at an advertised cost of 700,000 yen. Grew characterizes the film as dull and crude despite magnificent scenery, revealing that German director Dr. Arnold Fanck disowned the final product after facing continuous Japanese official interference and pressure from the German Embassy. Enclosed are three clippings from The Japan Advertiser: Esther Crane's premiere review describing the royal attendance of Prince and Princess Chichibu, and two comprehensive critical reviews by H. Vere Redman analyzing the film's artistic contradictions, moral compromises regarding romantic love versus filial duty, and variations between the German and Japanese cuts.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 2267: Japanese Propaganda Film, "The New Earth"

subfiles.about: Memorandum of conversation recording Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer's refusal to insert a Japanese political prologue into screenings of 'The Good Earth'.
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine (Department of State) and William A. Orr (Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer)
subfiles.summary: William A. Orr of Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer consults with Joseph W. Ballantine regarding demands made by the Japanese Home Office Censor Bureau on the film 'The Good Earth'. While accepting technical scene cuts, MGM refuses to attach a compulsory political prologue blaming the Nanking Government, Kuomintang, and Comintern for Chinese suffering and justifying Japanese military intervention. Ballantine advises Orr against making retaliatory publicity threats, recommending instead a courteous appeal to the principle of corporate political neutrality while discreetly hinting at potential negative public sentiment in the United States. Attached are letters from Tokyo manager Julian D. Berman, clippings quoting Viscount Hidemaro Konoye's claim in Bungei Shunju that the film was Chinese propaganda, the English translation of the demanded prologue, and detailed lists of cuts ordered by the Home Office and Yokohama Customs censors.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum of Conversation: Censorship of the Film "Good Earth" in Japan

subfiles.about: Instruction transmitting to the American Embassy in Tokyo the memorandum of conversation concerning censorship of 'The Good Earth'.
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State (drafted by Joseph W. Ballantine)
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State transmits to the American Embassy in Tokyo a copy of the memorandum of conversation of December 7, 1937, between William A. Orr of Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer and Joseph W. Ballantine. The transmittal provides the Embassy with background on Japanese censorship demands and the distributor's stance against exhibiting political propaganda.
subfiles.title: State Department Instruction to Tokyo Embassy Transmitting Memorandum on "The Good Earth"

subfiles.about: Letter alerting the State Department to Japanese emergency import laws prohibiting film imports and outlining a proposed credit syndicate.
subfiles.from: Frederick L. Herron, Foreign Manager, Motion Picture Producers & Distributors of America, Inc.
subfiles.summary: Frederick L. Herron alerts Maxwell M. Hamilton to an upcoming meeting in New York with Japanese government representatives regarding new statutory restrictions on film imports enacted under Japan's Emergency Import/Export Control Law of September 1937. Herron encloses his circular to Arthur M. Loew of Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer explaining that motion picture films and equipment are among 647 prohibited items subject to dictatorial Finance Ministry control. The Japanese proposal envisions an American export syndicate selling to a Japanese import syndicate financed by three-year, 6 percent dollar bank notes issued by U.S. branches of Japanese banks. Herron compares this system to the state monopoly established in Manchukuo, expressing concern that American distributors will be forced out of Japan and occupied China.
subfiles.title: Letter from Frederick L. Herron to Maxwell M. Hamilton on Japanese Film Import Control
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Letter acknowledging receipt of information regarding proposed Japanese film import restrictions and offering Department assistance.
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, Acting Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Joseph W. Ballantine acknowledges Frederick L. Herron's letter of December 23, 1937, addressed to Maxwell M. Hamilton. He expresses appreciation for the details provided regarding the import and financing scheme proposed by Japanese representatives for the January 4 meeting in New York. Ballantine asks to be informed of the outcome of the discussions and offers the Department's assistance if needed.
subfiles.title: Letter from Joseph W. Ballantine to Frederick L. Herron
subfiles.to: Frederick L. Herron, Motion Picture Producers & Distributors of America, Inc.

subfiles.about: Letter transmitting correspondence and proposals exchanged with Hisaji Kubo regarding a credit scheme for importing American films into Japan.
subfiles.from: Frederick L. Herron, Foreign Manager, Motion Picture Producers & Distributors of America, Inc.
subfiles.summary: Frederick L. Herron reports to Joseph W. Ballantine on conferences held in New York with Hisaji Kubo regarding a mechanism for resuming film imports into Japan. Herron describes Kubo as overbearing and lacking official governmental authority, noting that while Kubo claims Ministry of Finance backing, any workable arrangement must be negotiated directly through the distributors' Film Board of Trade in Tokyo. Enclosed are Herron's letter of January 10 to Kubo providing an introduction to Paramount representative Perkins in Japan, Kubo's letter of January 9, and Kubo's seven-point 'Plan for the Resumption of Film Imports into Japan' proposing three-year dollar promissory notes at 3 percent interest and an exclusive import association.
subfiles.title: Letter from Frederick L. Herron to Joseph W. Ballantine regarding Negotiations with Hisaji Kubo
subfiles.to: Joseph W. Ballantine, Acting Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Letter acknowledging receipt of correspondence regarding film import negotiations with Hisaji Kubo.
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Maxwell M. Hamilton acknowledges Frederick L. Herron's letter of January 12, 1938, enclosing correspondence exchanged with Hisaji Kubo. Hamilton expresses appreciation for keeping the Department of State informed of the progress of negotiations concerning the admission of American films into Japan.
subfiles.title: Letter from Maxwell M. Hamilton to Frederick L. Herron
subfiles.to: Frederick L. Herron, Motion Picture Producers & Distributors of America, Inc.

subfiles.about: Covering letter transmitting a confidential report from an American motion picture company representative in Japan.
subfiles.from: Frederick L. Herron, Foreign Manager, Motion Picture Producers & Distributors of America, Inc.
subfiles.summary: Frederick L. Herron transmits to Wallace Murray, Chief of the Division of Near Eastern Affairs (routed to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs), a copy of a report recently received by an American film company from its representative in Japan. The attached report continues on subsequent pages of the file.
subfiles.title: Letter from Frederick L. Herron to Wallace Murray Transmitting Report from Japan
subfiles.to: Wallace Murray, Chief, Division of Near Eastern Affairs, Department of State
